title: Kava extract for treating anxiety
citationText: Pittler MH, Ernst E. Kava extract for treating anxiety. Cochrane Database Syst Rev. 2003;(1):CD003383.
notes: Baseline provenance recovery for normalized enrichment. Exact legacy sourceId preserved; the review is dated and should not be treated as a freshness signal for new claims.

title: Kava for the treatment of generalized anxiety disorder RCT: analysis of adverse reactions, liver function, addiction, and sexual effects
citationText: Sarris J, et al. Kava for the treatment of generalized anxiety disorder RCT: analysis of adverse reactions, liver function, addiction, and sexual effects. Phytother Res. 2013;27(11):1723-1728.
notes: Six-week double-blind randomized trial in 75 adults with generalized anxiety disorder using Kava tablets providing 120 mg kavalactones/day, titrated in nonresponders to 240 mg/day. No significant group differences in liver function tests and no significant adverse reactions attributable to Kava were reported. This does not establish long-term safety, exclude rare hepatotoxicity, or establish safety in pre-existing liver disease.

title: EPIDIOLEX (cannabidiol) oral solution — 2021 prescribing information
citationText: U.S. Food and Drug Administration. EPIDIOLEX (cannabidiol) oral solution prescribing information. 2021 labeling revision.
notes: Inactive historical provenance only. Retained so deprecated audit records remain traceable; it must not support current publishable claims because newer EPIDIOLEX labeling is available.

title: EPIDIOLEX (cannabidiol) oral solution — prescribing information
citationText: U.S. Food and Drug Administration. EPIDIOLEX (cannabidiol) oral solution prescribing information. Revised May 2026.
notes: Current labeling revised 05/2026. Sections 7.2 and 7.4 support CYP2C19-substrate interaction and additive CNS-depressant sedation cautions for prescription cannabidiol.

title: Anti-inflammatory effects of luteolin: A review of in vitro, in vivo, and in silico studies
citationText: Aziz N, Kim MY, Cho JY. Anti-inflammatory effects of luteolin: A review of in vitro, in vivo, and in silico studies. J Ethnopharmacol. 2018;225:342-358.
notes: Baseline provenance recovery. Taxonomized as preclinical-mechanistic because the review is dominated by in-vitro, in-vivo, and in-silico evidence; it must not be counted as direct human efficacy evidence.

citationText: Hieu TH, et al. Therapeutic efficacy and safety of chamomile for state anxiety, generalized anxiety disorder, insomnia, and sleep quality: a systematic review and meta-analysis. Phytother Res. 2019;33(6):1604-1615.

title: An investigation into the stress-relieving and pharmacological actions of an ashwagandha (Withania somnifera) extract: A randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled study
citationText: Lopresti AL, Smith SJ, Malvi H, Kodgule R. An investigation into the stress-relieving and pharmacological actions of an ashwagandha extract: a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled study. Medicine (Baltimore). 2019;98(37):e17186.
notes: Baseline provenance recovery. Small 60-day Shoden trial in stressed healthy adults. The article reports no adverse events; acknowledgements state Arjuna Natural Ltd funded the project and supplied the extract, so null safety findings require sponsorship and sample-size context.

title: The Effectiveness and Safety of Cannabidiol in Non-seizure-related Indications: A Systematic Review of Published Randomized Clinical Trials
citationText: Tang Y, Tonkovich KL, Rudisill TM. The Effectiveness and Safety of Cannabidiol in Non-seizure-related Indications: A Systematic Review of Published Randomized Clinical Trials. Pharmaceut Med. 2022;36(6):353-385.
notes: Systematic review of 58 randomized studies outside seizure disorders. It found highly variable effectiveness, mostly small studies, and called for larger diverse samples and clearer dosing guidance; authors reported no relevant competing interests.

title: Preliminary Evidence on Safety and Clinical Efficacy of Luteolin for Patients With Prostate Cancer Under Active Surveillance
citationText: Naiki T, et al. Preliminary Evidence on Safety and Clinical Efficacy of Luteolin for Patients With Prostate Cancer Under Active Surveillance. Prostate Cancer. 2025;2025:8165686.
notes: Single-arm phase I study in five men with low/intermediate-risk localized prostate cancer under active surveillance using 50 mg oral luteolin daily for 180 days. Primary endpoint was safety; no symptomatic adverse events and no significant hematologic or serum-chemistry changes were reported. Oncologic outcomes were mixed (2 favorable, 1 stable, 2 progressed), so this source must not be generalized into efficacy or broad safety. Authors declared no conflicts; DHC Corporation supplied the 50 mg luteolin supplements. Funding was listed from JSPS KAKENHI, the Nitto Foundation, and the Aichi Health Promotion Foundation.

title: Cannabidiol and Liver Enzyme Level Elevations in Healthy Adults: A Randomized Clinical Trial
citationText: Florian J, et al. Cannabidiol and Liver Enzyme Level Elevations in Healthy Adults: A Randomized Clinical Trial. JAMA Intern Med. 2025;185(9):1070-1078.
notes: Baseline provenance recovery for normalized enrichment. FDA-led randomized trial in healthy adults; exact legacy sourceId preserved.

title: Safety of 8-Week Administration With Ashwagandha (Withania somnifera) Root Extract in Adults With Stress and Anxiety: Findings From a Prospective, Randomized, Multi-Center, Double-Blinded, Placebo-Controlled Study
citationText: Safety of 8-Week Administration With Ashwagandha (Withania somnifera) Root Extract in Adults With Stress and Anxiety. Phytother Res. 2026;40(8):5005-5015.
notes: PMCID PMC13436282. Randomized double-blind placebo-controlled multicenter/multinational safety study in 1002 adults aged 18-65 with borderline-to-moderate anxiety and elevated stress. The studied product was root-only KSM-66 extract standardized to >5% total withanolides and <0.1% withaferin A, 300 mg twice daily (600 mg/day) for eight weeks. No serious adverse events or significant between-group liver, renal, or hematologic laboratory changes were reported, but tolerability did not differ significantly (p=0.487), paired laboratory data were incomplete, biomarker depth and follow-up were limited, and recruitment was predominantly in India. This source does not establish comparative efficacy, exclude rare or longer-latency injury, or support other products, doses, durations, or populations. Shri Kartikeya Pharma supported the study; Ixoreal Biomed supplied KSM-66; authors declared no conflicts of interest.

title: Safety of cannabidiol versus placebo in healthy population: a systematic review and meta-analysis
citationText: Sawaira F, et al. Safety of cannabidiol versus placebo in healthy population: a systematic review and meta-analysis. Ann Med Surg (Lond). 2026;88(3):2348-2356.
notes: Systematic review and meta-analysis of four randomized placebo-controlled trials involving 269 healthy adults. Diarrhea was higher with cannabidiol (RR 5.85, 95% CI 1.14–30.02; P=0.03); abdominal pain and headache trends were not statistically significant, and fatigue, dizziness, and upper respiratory tract infection did not differ significantly. Exposures were heterogeneous and short-term, so the study does not establish a general dose or long-term safety. PMCID PMC12959810. The authors declared no conflict of interest.

title: Acute oral sodium propionate supplementation raises resting energy expenditure and lipid oxidation in fasted humans
citationText: Chambers ES, et al. Acute oral sodium propionate supplementation raises resting energy expenditure and lipid oxidation in fasted humans. Diabetes Obes Metab. 2018;20(4):1034-1039.
notes: PMCID PMC5873405. Randomized crossover study in 18 healthy adults after an overnight fast. Sodium propionate tablets totaling 6845 mg over 180 minutes acutely increased resting energy expenditure and whole-body lipid oxidation without changing glucose or insulin. This is acute surrogate physiology and does not establish durable weight loss, chronic metabolic efficacy, or a consumer dosing recommendation.

title: Acute effects of the food preservative propionic acid on glucose metabolism in humans
citationText: Adler GK, et al. Acute effects of the food preservative propionic acid on glucose metabolism in humans. BMJ Open Diabetes Res Care. 2021;9(1):e002336.
notes: PMCID PMC8314753. Randomized placebo-controlled crossover study in 28 healthy adults following a one-week propionic-acid-free diet. A 1500 mg calcium propionate preservative-exposure model increased counter-regulatory hormones and, under hypoglycemic clamp conditions, endogenous glucose production. This exposure-specific acute signal must not be generalized to endogenous microbiota-derived propionate, other salts, other delivery systems, or chronic clinical outcomes. The article reports no competing interests.

title: Increase in colonic propionate as a method of preventing weight gain in adults aged 20–40 years: iPREVENT, a multicentre, double-blind, randomised, parallel-group trial
citationText: Frost G, et al. Increase in colonic propionate as a method of preventing weight gain in adults aged 20–40 years: iPREVENT, a multicentre, double-blind, randomised, parallel-group trial. Efficacy and Mechanism Evaluation. 2025;12(8).
notes: NIHR Efficacy and Mechanism Evaluation report indexed in PubMed (Bookshelf ID NBK616126). Multicentre double-blind randomized trial in 270 adults aged 20–40 years at risk of weight gain. Inulin-propionate ester 10 g/day did not prevent weight gain versus 10 g/day inulin over 12 months; most body-composition and fasting biomarker outcomes did not differ. The engineered colon-targeted ester and active inulin control are not interchangeable with generic oral propionate, propionate salts, preservative exposure, endogenous microbiota-derived propionate, or other delivery routes.
